In the 
United States Court of Appeals 
For the Eleventh Circuit 
____________________ 
No. 26-14027 ____________________ 
JESSE GUARDADO, 
Plaintiff-Appellant, 
versus 
SECRETARY, DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, 
WARDEN, FLORIDA STATE PRISON, 
Defendants-Appellees. 
____________________ 
Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Middle District of Florida 
D.C. Docket No. 3:26-cv-02596-MMH-SJH ____________________ 
Before WILLIAM PRYOR, Chief Judge, and JILL PRYOR and LUCK, Circuit Judges. 
BY THE COURT: 
On September 13, 2004, while he was on conditional release 
from an earlier stint in prison for armed robbery, Jesse Guardado 
beat Jackie Malone with a breaker bar and stabbed her with a knife, 
again and again and again, until she was dead so he could rob her 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 1 of 20

2 Order of the Court 26-14027 
and buy crack with the loot he stole. Guardado v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of 
Corr., 112 F.4th 958, 962–63 (11th Cir. 2024), cert. denied, 145 S. Ct. 
2822 (2025). Guardado’s guilt was never in doubt. He confessed 
and pleaded guilty. Id. at 963–64. 
After a penalty phase, the state trial court, following the 
jury’s unanimous recommendation, sentenced Guardado to death. 
Id. at 964–73. His direct appeals were denied. See Guardado v. State, 
965 So. 2d 108 (Fla. 2007), cert. denied, 552 U.S. 1197 (2008). And his 
state and federal postconviction challenges were also rejected. See
Guardado v. State, 176 So. 3d 886 (Fla. 2015); Guardado v. State, 238 
So. 3d 162 (Fla. 2018); Guardado, 112 F.4th at 995; Guardado v. State, 
—So. 3d—, 2026 WL 3267707 (Fla. Oct. 29, 2026). 
More than twenty years after his death sentence, and on the 
cusp of his execution on November 5, 2026, Guardado sued the 
Secretary of the Florida Department of Corrections and the Warden of Florida State Prison under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, claiming 
that the method the state will use to execute him violates his Eighth 
Amendment right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. 
The state’s lethal-injection protocol, Guardado alleged, is supposed 
to be administered in three stages. First comes a large dose of 
etomidate, which is a sedative that renders the prisoner unconscious and insensate to pain. Next is rocuronium bromide, which 
is a paralytic agent that keeps the prisoner from moving. The last 
drug is potassium acetate, which causes cardiac arrest. 
Guardado alleged that, in one of five ways, there’s a substantial risk the state will fail to administer properly this lethal-injection 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 2 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 3 
protocol: (1) the state will not use etomidate during the execution; 
(2) the state will use an insufficient amount of etomidate; (3) the 
state will use an expired dose of etomidate; (4) the state will use 
insufficient doses of the other two drugs; and (5) the state will use 
drugs that are not part of the protocol. As a result, Guardado alleged that there’s a substantial risk he will consciously suffocate 
during the execution, which would be cruel and unusual under the 
Eighth Amendment. Along with his complaint, Guardado moved 
to stay his execution while his method-of-execution claim was 
pending. 
The district court ordered limited discovery on the expired 
etomidate issue and held an evidentiary hearing on the stay motion. After the hearing, the court denied the motion because 
Guardado was not likely to succeed on the merits of his Eighth 
Amendment method-of-execution claim. “His concern regarding 
the potential use or future use of expired etomidate” was “not supported by the evidence,” the district court explained. “And his various other concerns [were] far too speculative to support a finding 
that [the state’s] planned execution protocol present[ed] a risk that 
[was] sure or very likely to cause serious illness or needless suffering.” 
Guardado has appealed the denial of his stay motion. And 
he has moved for a stay of execution pending his appeal. We take 
up that motion now. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 3 of 20

4 Order of the Court 26-14027 
I.
 “To obtain a stay of his execution pending appeal,” 
Guardado “must show that ‘(1) he has a substantial likelihood of 
success on the merits’ of his appeal, ‘(2) he will suffer irreparable 
injury unless the injunction issues; (3) the stay would not substantially harm the other litigant; and (4) if issued, the injunction would 
not be adverse to the public interest.’” See Humphreys v. Comm’r, 
Ga. Dep’t of Corr., 161 F.4th 1300, 1306 (11th Cir. 2025) (quoting 
James v. Sec’y, Dep’t of Corr., 130 F.4th 1291, 1295 (11th Cir. 2025)). 
We start with the first stay factor. 
II. 
 “A death row inmate may attempt to show that a [s]tate’s 
planned method of execution, either on its face or as applied to 
him, violates the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on ‘cruel and 
unusual’ punishment.” Nance v. Ward, 142 S. Ct. 2215, 2219–20 
(2022). “To succeed on that claim . . . he must satisfy two requirements.” Id. at 2220. “First, he must establish that the [s]tate’s 
method of execution presents a ‘substantial risk of serious harm’—
severe pain over and above death itself.” Id. (quoting Glossip v. 
Gross, 576 U.S. 863, 877 (2015)). Second, “he ‘must identify an alternative [method] that is feasible, readily implemented, and in fact 
significantly reduce[s]’ the risk of harm involved.” Id. (alterations 
in original) (quoting Glossip, 576 U.S. at 877). 
A. 
As to the first requirement, Guardado argues that there’s a 
substantial risk the state will improperly apply its lethal-injection 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 4 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 5 
protocol during his execution. This will happen in one of five ways, 
he says: (1) the state will not administer etomidate; (2) the state 
will not administer enough etomidate to render him unconscious; 
(3) the state will use expired etomidate; (4) the state will use insufficient dosages of the other two drugs in the protocol; and (5) the 
state will use unlisted drugs in addition to the three called for under 
the protocol. Misapplying the protocol, Guardado contends, will 
result in a substantial risk that he will consciously suffocate. 
Guardado has not met his burden on the first method-of-execution requirement. As to each alleged misapplication, the district 
court found that there was no substantial likelihood that Guardado 
was “sure or very likely” to experience needless suffering. Having 
carefully reviewed the record, we believe these findings were not 
clearly erroneous. See Brooks v. Warden, 810 F.3d 812, 824 (11th Cir. 
2016) (reviewing findings made by the district court in denying a 
stay of execution for clear error); Grayson v. Allen, 491 F.3d 1318, 
1324–25 (11th Cir. 2007) (same). 
1. 
Guardado first contends the state will not use etomidate during his execution. In support, he points to the drug log entries for 
three prisoners—Thomas Gudinas, Michael Bell, and Edward 
Zakrzewski—showing no documented removal of etomidate from 
the state’s pharmacy for their executions. From this, Guardado assumes that the three prisoners must not have been administered 
etomidate during their executions. And, he argues, there’s a substantial risk the same will happen to him. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 5 of 20

6 Order of the Court 26-14027 
But Guardado’s assumption is off. The district court found 
that the three prisoners did receive etomidate during their executions and the drug log entries were merely recordkeeping errors. 
Its finding was well supported by the evidence. See Grayson v. 
Comm’r, Ala. Dep’t of Corr., 121 F.4th 894, 896 (11th Cir. 2024) (Under “clear error review,” “a finding ‘that is plausible in light of the 
full record—even if another is equally or more so—must govern.’” 
(quoting Cooper v. Harris, 581 U.S. 285, 293 (2017))). Agent Adam 
Graff, a state law enforcement officer who participated in Bell’s execution, testified that etomidate was administered. And the postexecution toxicology reports for the three prisoners undisputably 
showed that they had etomidate in their blood after the executions. 
That could only have come from administration of etomidate during their executions. So, we know as a scientific fact that they received the first drug in the protocol. 
2. 
Next, Guardado asserts that the state will not give him 
enough etomidate to render him unconscious, which means 
there’s a substantial risk he will consciously suffocate as the other 
two drugs are administered. He cites the post-execution toxicology 
reports of two prisoners—Bell and Samuel Smithers—which show 
a tenfold disparity in post-mortem etomidate levels between them. 
And he points to disparities (albeit much smaller) in the post-execution toxicology reports of other prisoners. Guardado contends 
that the lower blood levels show that the prisoners received less 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 6 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 7 
etomidate than would be necessary to render them unconscious 
during their executions. 
Guardado’s contention assumes that the prisoners’ postmortem blood levels would have been similar to the etomidate in 
their blood at the time of their executions. Yet the science does not 
back up his assumption. As the district court observed, the etomidate level to render someone insensate and unconscious is measured based on plasma blood. But the toxicology reports Guardado 
relies on measured “whole blood,” which is “‘absolutely not’ a oneto-one measurement.” The comparison fails out of the gate. 
And as the district court further found, post-mortem blood 
levels don’t tell us much about the drug levels at the time of the 
execution because, even after death, drugs redistribute and metabolize in the body, which impacts toxicology blood levels that are 
taken hours later. The record evidence supports this finding. 
Guardado’s medical expert conceded that “[p]ost[-]mortem drug 
redistribution [i.e., circulation] is well known, and post[-]mortem 
drug concentrations may be unreliable proxies for circulating 
blood levels while alive.” And the state’s medical expert explained 
that post-mortem readings do not reflect conditions during the execution because etomidate continues circulating and degrading in 
the blood for some period after death. Post-mortem etomidate levels also depend on individual prisoners’ unique “physiological 
makeup,” like their metabolisms, health conditions, and body compositions, making comparisons between individuals even more difficult. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 7 of 20

8 Order of the Court 26-14027 
3. 
Guardado also maintains that the state will likely use expired 
etomidate during his execution. He relies on drug log entries 
showing that expired etomidate was used in six executions in 2025. 
Expired etomidate loses its potency, he explains, which creates a 
substantial risk that it will be ineffective to render him unconscious 
during the execution. 
But the district court found these entries were also recordkeeping errors, and the record supports this finding. The state’s 
chief of pharmaceutical services, Dr. Renea Marcano, testified that 
the 2025 expiration dates on the logs were mistaken. The expiration dates should have been listed as January 2027 because that is 
when the etomidate will actually expire. Two law enforcement 
officers, Agent Graff and Agent Kevin James, saw the vials of etomidate before they were administered in five of the six executions and 
the agents confirmed that they were not expired. And the state’s 
receipts and lot numbers for its stock of etomidate showed that the 
etomidate used in the six executions had an expiration date of January 2027. In fact, the state never had etomidate with a January 31, 
2025 expiration date, as the mistaken entries had shown. 
As to Guardado’s execution, specifically, Dr. Marcano 
averred that she had set aside the proper dose of etomidate, and the 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 8 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 9 
expiration date was January 2027. So, there is no substantial likelihood that the state will use expired etomidate for his execution.1
4. 
Additionally, Guardado contends that there’s a substantial 
risk he will not receive proper doses of the other two drugs in the 
lethal-injection protocol. In support, he highlights the drug log entries showing the doses of rocuronium bromide and potassium acetate withdrawn for the executions of two prisoners—Anthony 
Wainwright and Gudinas—were less than the amount required by 
the protocol. 
But as the district court found, there was no substantial risk 
of serious harm to Guardado from the lower doses of the other two 
drugs because the etomidate would render him insensate during 
his execution. He would never know he received less of the other 
two drugs than he was supposed to because he would be deeply 
unconscious (based on the amount of etomidate the prisoner is 
given under the protocol). 
Guardado speculates that “an insufficient dosage of one drug 
could lead to unnecessary suffering from another,” but there’s no 
evidence in the record to support his speculation. And even if there 
were evidence to support it, Guardado has to show a substantial 
1 The district court also found that, at best for Guardado, expired etomidate 
has only the “potential” to degrade, which was insufficient to show a substantial risk of serious harm. Guardado does not address this finding in his stay 
motion. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 9 of 20

10 Order of the Court 26-14027 
risk of serious harm. See Glossip, 576 U.S. at 877. Could is not 
enough. 
5. 
Finally, Guardado argues that there’s a substantial risk the 
state will use lidocaine (a drug not listed in the protocol) during his 
execution, in addition to the other three drugs in the protocol. He 
draws this inference from the state’s drug logs, which show that 
lidocaine was removed from the pharmacy and taken to the prison 
where the state conducts the executions. 
But as the district court found, Guardado “fail[ed] to present 
evidence to support th[e] notion” that the state’s “rare use of lidocaine” would “cause needless suffering.” Dr. Marcano testified 
that lidocaine is used only if the state needs to get access to a prisoner’s vein through a cutdown procedure as outlined in the lethalinjection protocol. The lidocaine, which is a local anesthetic, is on 
the medical cart in the execution chamber in case the cutdown happens. 
But the state has not “done a cutdown in a long time.” And 
Agent Graff testified that in all the thirteen executions he’s witnessed, he had never seen lidocaine used in an execution. There is 
no evidence—and Guardado does not argue—that he will need a 
cutdown procedure for his execution. So, there is no substantial 
likelihood that lidocaine will be used on him. In any event, while 
Guardado’s expert witnesses testified that using lidocaine “could” 
lead to seizures and other life-threatening conditions, the unspecified chance that lidocaine could cause a problem for some prisoners 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 10 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 11 
is not enough to show a substantial risk of that result as required 
under the Eighth Amendment. Guardado has not shown a substantial likelihood of success on the first requirement of his 
method-of-execution claim. 
B. 
And his stay motion is silent on the second requirement. To 
obtain a stay on a method-of-execution claim, Guardado has the 
burden to show a substantial likelihood that there’s a feasible, readily implemented, alternative method-of-execution that will significantly reduce the substantial risk of serious harm from the maladministration of the lethal-injection protocol. See Nance, 142 S. Ct. 
at 2220. Guardado submitted a firing squad as his preferred alternative below. But his stay motion doesn’t mention anything about 
a feasible and readily implemented alternative method of execution. Not once. Nor does it explain why his failure to proffer an 
alternative is excusable. This failure to address a necessary element 
of his claim is fatal to a stay. 
C.
While he doesn’t mention the second requirement of his 
method-of-execution claim, Guardado does make an additional argument for why he’s entitled to a stay. The district court, he contends, curtailed the discovery process and held a compressed evidentiary hearing, which made it hard to carry his burden. 
But “[a] district court has wide discretion in discovery matters and our review is accordingly deferential.” Arthur v. Comm’r, 
Ala. Dep’t of Corr., 840 F.3d 1268, 1304 (11th Cir. 2016) (quoting 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 11 of 20

12 Order of the Court 26-14027 
Bradley v. King, 556 F.3d 1225, 1229 (11th Cir. 2009)). “[A] district 
court’s denial of additional discovery must result in substantial 
harm to a party’s case in order to establish an abuse of discretion.” 
Id. (quoting Bradley, 556 F.3d at 1229). 
There is no substantial harm here. The district court allowed limited discovery on the state’s use of expired etomidate, requiring the state to turn over updated drug logs showing drug 
names, withdrawal dates, and expiration dates through the present. 
And even before that order, the state had already filed as exhibits 
state execution checklists and autopsy/toxicology reports for a 
number of prisoners, and had filed a list of expert and fact witnesses 
who would speak to execution protocol and pharmaceutical 
recordkeeping. The district court later ordered the state to submit 
for in camera review unredacted drug logs showing the lot and invoice numbers from when the state purchased the etomidate. And 
it held an evidentiary hearing where Guardado had the opportunity to present the testimony of two expert witnesses and to 
cross-examine the state’s expert and fact witnesses. 
Other than arguing that his “claim necessitated further discovery and inquiry into [the state’s] practices,” Guardado does not 
detail the substantial harm he suffered from the district court’s discovery rulings.2 “Considering the district court’s broad discretion, 
2 In his reply in support of the stay motion, Guardado reiterates that he 
“learned additional new facts that . . . called for further development.” But 
other than referencing the use of lidocaine—which he already knew about and 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 12 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 13 
we cannot say its decision about discovery resulted in substantial 
harm to [Guardado’s] case.” See id. at 1305 (citation modified). 
III. 
The other factors also weigh against staying Guardado’s execution. “[B]efore granting a stay of execution, a court must ‘consider not only the likelihood of success on the merits . . . but also 
the extent to which the inmate has delayed unnecessarily in bringing the claim.” Long v. Sec’y, Dep’t of Corr., 924 F.3d 1171, 1176 (11th 
Cir. 2019) (quoting Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 649–50 (2004)). 
“There is a ‘strong equitable presumption against the grant of a stay 
where a claim could have been brought at such a time as to allow 
consideration of the merits without requiring entry of a stay.’” Id.
(quoting Nelson, 541 U.S. at 650). 
 Here, Guardado could have raised his method-of-execution 
claim at least nine months earlier when Frank Walls brought a similar Eighth Amendment claim based on some of the same records 
that Guardado relies on.3 He could have raised his claim eight 
was alleged in his complaint—he doesn’t explain what the further development would show. 
3 In his reply, Guardado argues that he filed his method-of-execution claim “at 
the earliest opportunity, just weeks after he became warrant-eligible.” But 
Guardado is mistaken. In Florida, a prisoner sentenced to death is “warranteligible” after initial state and federal postconviction proceedings are completed. Cf. Silvia v. State, 228 So. 3d 1144, 1146 (Fla. 2013) (“The transcript 
further reflects that Silvia understood that if the court granted his request to 
discharge his attorneys and waive postconviction proceedings, he would become warrant-eligible—that is, the governor could sign a warrant for his execution.”); Jones v. State, 419 So. 3d 619, 625–26 (Fla. 2025) (“[T]he Clerk of this 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 13 of 20

14 Order of the Court 26-14027 
months earlier when Ronald Heath brought a similar method-ofexecution claim in state court based on similar evidence. See Heath 
v. State, 426 So. 3d 1253, 1261–62 (Fla. 2026) (describing similar 
claim). And he could have raised his claim seven months earlier 
when Melvin Trotter brought a similar claim in state court based 
on similar evidence. See Trotter v. State, 428 So. 3d 68, 71–73 (Fla. 
2026) (describing a similar claim). Instead, Guardado delayed more 
than half-a-year before raising his method-of-execution claim. 
 “We have refused to grant stays in cases involving delayed 
filings before, and [Guardado’s] delay was even more pronounced 
and less justifiable.” See Long, 924 F.3d at 1178 (citing Brooks, 810 
F.3d at 826; In re Hutcherson, 468 F.3d 747, 749–50 (11th Cir. 2006); 
Diaz v. McDonough, 472 F.3d 849, 851 (11th Cir. 2006); Jones v. Allen, 
485 F.3d 635, 640 (11th Cir. 2007)). We refuse to do so here as well. 
 Guardado argues that we shouldn’t refuse because the state 
didn’t move forward with the execution warrant until after he filed 
his claim. But pointing to when the state issued the warrant 
Court certified to the Governor on October 4, 2013, that Jones had completed 
his direct appeal and initial postconviction proceedings in state court and his 
habeas corpus proceedings and appeal therefrom in federal court. Thus, in 
addition to the thirty-two years of notice since the imposition of his death sentences, Jones has been on notice for nearly twelve years that he is ‘warranteligible,’ meaning ‘the [G]overnor could sign a warrant for his execution.’” 
(citation modified)). Guardado became warrant-eligible in 2025 when the Supreme Court denied certiorari review in his federal postconviction appeal. See
Guardado, 145 S. Ct. at 2822. In any event, the accrual of Guardado’s methodof-execution claim—which is when he could have brought his claim—is not 
the same as his warrant-eligibility. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 14 of 20

26-14027 Order of the Court 15 
doesn’t answer or explain why he delayed nine months to bring his 
claim. Because he offers no explanation, we should apply the 
strong equitable presumption against granting the stay. 
 “The remainder of the factors we apply when considering a 
stay amount to a weighing of the equitable interests of [Guardado], 
the [state], and the public.” See Ray v. Comm’r, Ala. Dep’t of Corr., 
915 F.3d 689, 701 (11th Cir. 2019). On the state and the public’s 
side of the scale, “the Supreme Court has recognized [that] the 
state, the victim, and the victim’s family . . . ‘have an important interest in the timely enforcement of [Guardado’s] sentence.’” See
Brooks, 810 F.3d at 825 (quoting Hill v. McDonough, 547 U.S. 573, 584 
(2006)). “[E]quity must be sensitive to the [s]tate’s strong interest 
in enforcing its criminal judgments without undue interference 
from the federal courts.” Hill, 547 U.S. at 584. For that reason, “we 
have rejected the argument that” a prisoner “will suffer irreparable 
harm if he is executed, whereas the state will only suffer a minimal 
inconvenience, because the state, the victim, and the victim’s family also have an important interest in the timely enforcement of 
[the prisoner’s] sentence.” Bowles v. DeSantis, 934 F.3d 1230, 1247–
48 (11th Cir. 2019) (citation modified). 
IV. 
Because Guardado has not shown a substantial likelihood 
that he will prevail in his appeal, and the other equitable factors 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 15 of 20

16 Order of the Court 26-14027 
caution against granting a stay, we DENY his motion for a stay of 
execution.4
MOTION DENIED. 
4 We GRANT Guardado’s motion to proceed in forma pauperis. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 16 of 20

26-14027 JILL PRYOR, J., Concurring 1 
JILL PRYOR, Circuit Judge, Concurring: 
 So far this year, Florida has executed eighteen prisoners. 
Later this week, it plans to execute Jesse Guardado. It plans to carry 
out his execution using the same protocol it used for its other executions this year. During the execution, Florida will administer to 
Mr. Guardado three drugs: etomidate (a sedative), rocuronium bromide (a paralytic agent), and potassium acetate (which causes cardiac arrest). 
Before Florida obtained a warrant to execute Mr. Guardado, 
he filed a lawsuit in federal court making a constitutional challenge 
to his execution. The primary basis for his method-of-execution 
challenge was his claim that Florida had used expired etomidate in 
earlier executions and would use the expired drug for his execution, 
which would result in him being awake and aware during the administration of the other two drugs. 
The basis for Guardado’s troubling allegations was, at least 
in part, inventory records from the Florida Department of Corrections. The Department’s Chief of Pharmacy Services oversees the 
storage of the drugs used in executions and maintains logs concerning the storage of each drug. When the Department acquires 
a supply of one of the drugs, it records on a log the date it acquired 
the drug, the vendor who provided the drug, the lot number of the 
drug, the expiration date of the drug, and the quantity of the drug. 
The log is also supposed to reflect each time the Department uses 
any of its inventory of a drug, such as when it carries out an execution. It is undisputed that the logs the Department maintained 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 17 of 20

2 JILL PRYOR, J., Concurring 26-14027 
showed that Florida had used expired etomidate in several previous 
executions and, for three more executions, included no entries 
showing that it had used any etomidate at all. 
After discovery and an evidentiary hearing on Mr. 
Guardado’s claim, the district court found that the Department was 
not using expired etomidate or failing to administer the drug at all. 
Based on its findings of fact, the district court correctly concluded 
that Mr. Guardado has not shown a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of his method-of-execution claim. I agree with 
the majority that based on the district court’s fact findings, which 
are not clearly erroneous, Mr. Guardado is not entitled to a stay of 
his execution. Accordingly, I join parts I, II.A, II.C, and IV of the 
Court’s order.1
Still, this case has brought to light concerning facts about the 
Florida Department of Corrections’ failure to maintain accurate 
records for drugs used in its executions. We now know that the Department of Corrections was not taking care to ensure that its logs 
contained accurate information. Testimony from the evidentiary 
hearing showed that the person preparing the logs improperly recorded the expiration date of the etomidate because English was not 
his first language, and he did not understand that the log was requesting the expiration date for the drug, not the current year. 
1 I do not join parts II.B or III, which address whether Mr. Guardado has shown 
a feasible alternative method of execution and whether factors other than substantial likelihood of success on the merits support a stay, respectively. It is 
unnecessary to address these issues to decide the appeal before us. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 18 of 20

26-14027 JILL PRYOR, J., Concurring 3 
But even more concerning is Florida’s response once it 
learned during litigation about the errors in its drug log. When the 
Department realized that its logs contained inaccurate information 
about drug expiration dates, its solution was to use Wite-Out liquid 
eraser to alter the logs. It did not make any attempt to document 
either in the log or elsewhere that a change had been made to the 
log, when the change was made, who made the change, or why the 
change had been made. The evidence in this case shows that these 
types of untraceable edits to a log tracking the storage of a drug is 
“completely inappropriate” and indeed “invalidates the point[] of 
the records,” which should be a contemporaneous record of each 
drug that was acquired and used. Doc. 54 at 30, 41.2 
Although the recordkeeping failures in this case do not rise 
to the level of a constitutional tort, the State’s lack of transparency 
and failure to maintain accurate records is deeply concerning. It 
would be troubling if a State pharmacy failed to adequately track 
the storage of drugs in its possession. But, here, the failure occurred with the storage of drugs used to carry out executions. In 
this context, a State must maintain accurate and thorough records 
of its practices to be able to demonstrate that it is carrying out executions according to its protocols and in compliance with the Constitution. As Justice Sotomayor recently emphasized in another 
Florida case, such records are needed to “instill[] confidence in the 
[execution] protocol for everyone—prisoners, the courts, and the 
public alike.” Trotter v. Florida, 146 S. Ct. 755, 756 (2026) 
2 “Doc.” numbers refer to the district court’s docket entries. 
USCA11 Case: 26-14027 Document: 13-1 Date Filed: 11/02/2026 Page: 19 of 20

4 JILL PRYOR, J., Concurring 26-14027 
(Sotomayor, J., statement respecting the denial of the application 
for stay of execution and denial of certiorari). And, as this case 
demonstrates, a State’s failure to maintain accurate records will invariably lead to concerns and questions about whether the State is 
adhering to its protocol as well as the efficacy and constitutionality 
of that protocol. 
One final note. Our conclusion today that Mr. Guardado is 
not entitled to a stay of execution should not in any way signal or 
suggest that we condone the Department of Corrections’ failure to 
meet its basic responsibility to maintain accurate records.
